body: Architecture has always been shaped around people, and especially around the way they move. The coaching inn, the railway station, the bus depot, the airport and the highway service area were each built around a pause in a journey, and each was sized to the time that pause allowed. That pause is now changing. Fuel is getting more expensive, vehicles are learning to drive themselves, and road transport is turning to electricity. A car that once stopped for five minutes to fill its tank now stops for close to an hour to charge. Yet the places built for charging have hardly changed from the car parks and forecourts they replaced, and many drivers avoid them altogether by charging at home.

This thesis, the Powerhouse, proposes a sustainable charging cluster: an Electric Vehicle Powerhouse complex that will turn charging activities into an opportunity for enhanced civic / community engagements. It is not one building repeated along the highway. Each Powerhouse takes its programme from what the community around it lacks, and that programme is what brings people in; the charge is what lets them stay.
Nor is it only for electric vehicles. The Powerhouse is open to everyone, including people who arrive on foot, by bus or by bicycle.

Thousands of new charging sites will be built over the coming decades, and most are being planned as infrastructure and nothing more. This thesis asks how they could instead be woven into the everyday needs of the communities they sit in, and what it would take for those places to sustain themselves. It starts from a simple belief: that the energy transition is a chance to leave behind a better and greener landscape than the one we have now.

Transport uses a great deal of energy and wastes most of it. Of every hundred tonnes of greenhouse gas the United States emits, twenty-eight come from moving people and goods, more than from any other sector.<sup>1</sup> Across the world, road vehicles added just over six billion tonnes of carbon dioxide to the air in 2024.<sup>2</sup> Much of the problem is the engine. Fill a petrol car and roughly seven-tenths of that energy leaves through the exhaust and the radiator as heat; only about three-tenths actually moves the car. An electric car turns the ratio around, putting close to nine-tenths of what is in its battery to work.<sup>3</sup> At the wheels, it makes the same journey on roughly a third of the energy. Even so, an electric car is only as clean as the grid behind it. Economists who priced the damage done by driving electric across the United States found a clear benefit in California and a net harm in coal-heavy North Dakota.<sup>4</sup> This is one reason the Powerhouse generates its own energy.

The shift is happening fast. Five years ago electric cars were a niche of a few million sales a year. In 2025 buyers took home more than twenty million.<sup>5</sup> Automation is arriving alongside it. In ten American cities, Waymo now sells around half a million rides a week in cars with nobody at the wheel,<sup>6</sup> and since 2025 Aurora’s trucks have hauled paying freight between Dallas and Houston with the cab empty.<sup>7</sup> Cars have gone first. Freight and long-distance road transport are next. Speed is not the same as certainty, though. A review of ninety-four studies on electric-car adoption found that what actually persuades people to switch, public charging included, is far less settled than is usually assumed.<sup>8</sup>

For now, most charging happens at home. By the Department of Energy’s estimate, four of every five charges happen in a driveway or a garage.<sup>9</sup> That convenience has a cost. An electric car driven a typical American distance uses roughly three to four thousand kilowatt-hours of electricity a year, about a third of what an average home already uses.<sup>10</sup> Home charging moves the cost of the transition onto household bills, and is not an option for people who live in apartments or park on the street. Public charging will have to carry more of the load, and the places built for it will matter.

body: Every kind of travel has produced its own architecture of waiting. On the Silk Road the caravanserai gave shelter, trade and exchange at the end of a day’s march; along coaching roads the inn offered rest, food and news for travellers and the town alike. The great railway stations of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries were among the grandest civic buildings in their cities. Passengers arrived early and waited in vast halls, concourses and plazas, surrounded by restaurants, shops and newsstands. In New York, McKim, Mead and White borrowed the vaults of an ancient Roman bath for the waiting room of Pennsylvania Station (1910), and when Penn Station was demolished in 1963, New York lost its great civic room for the train and the city’s preservation movement began.<sup>11</sup> Airports went further, turning the terminal into a city of waiting.

The roadside stop went the other way. For most of the twentieth century it meant the gas station, which settled early into a formula that hardly changed afterwards: a roof over the pumps, islands to pull up beside, and a booth where you paid on the way out.<sup>12</sup> It was built for grab-and-go, and it did that well. Five minutes is long enough to pay and too short for a civic form.

The charging stop has inherited this form without its reason. The usual response is to add a few chargers to an existing car park. Public programmes such as the US National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure programme set standards for power and equipment, but say nothing about the place around the charger.<sup>13</sup> Drivers end up sitting in their cars beside a row of posts. Freight is worse off. American truckers already compete for somewhere to stop. Truck parking now ranks as the industry’s second most pressing problem after the economy, and drivers near the end of their legal hours often keep driving in search of a space.<sup>14</sup> Very few charging sites are built for heavy vehicles. A recent review of the American trucking market names charging infrastructure, alongside range and upfront cost, as one of the main obstacles to electric freight.<sup>15</sup> As trucks electrify, their stops will get longer, with nowhere designed to hold them. Marc Augé’s word for such spaces, non-places, fits them well: they are used all the time and belong to no one.<sup>16</sup>

A few operators have tried to do more. In England, Gridserve’s forecourt at Braintree set a café, a shop and a lounge beside its chargers in 2020,17 a glimpse of what a longer stop can support, though it is a commercial venture first. Japan has already proved the public version at national scale: since 1993 its Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism has designated more than 1,200 Michi-no-eki (“road stations”), each pairing free 24-hour parking, toilets and rest for travellers with a market for local produce, restaurants, crafts, events and disaster-relief facilities run with the municipality and local residents.18
notes: Carroll L. V. Meeks, The Railroad Station: An Architectural History (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1956).

body: How long a vehicle stops depends on what it is and how it charges. A fast charge takes twenty minutes to an hour; a slower charger at home or at a bus depot takes several hours, usually overnight. For freight, the stop is set by law as well as by technology: American rules require half an hour off after eight hours at the wheel, and ten hours off duty at the end of a working day.<sup>19</sup> An electric truck can charge during a break the driver already has to take. The thesis looks at all road transport, not only cars. Trucks, buses, motorcycles, bicycles and e-bikes all need somewhere to stop and charge, and each brings different people to the site. The Powerhouse plans for all of these stays, and fits its programme to them.
notes: Maximum Driving Time for Property-Carrying Vehicles, 49 C.F.R. § 395.3.

body: A long stay gives a site time, but not a reason to be there. Few kinds of land in America are as plentiful, or as idle, as the parking lot. The typical car stands still about 95 per cent of the time, and the lots that store it stand idle with it.<sup>20</sup> Parking is public infrastructure, built for one use and left empty for most of the day. The Powerhouse is the electric version of the parking lot. Its claim is that this ground can carry a civic or community amenity as well as cars.

Space alone does not make a place. For more than sixty years New York has let developers build bigger in return for a plaza or an arcade at street level. When Jerold Kayden’s team visited 503 of these spaces, they rated about two in every five as marginal.<sup>21</sup> William Whyte spent years filming people in plazas like these. He found that people stayed where there was something to do and somewhere to sit, and walked past everywhere else.<sup>22</sup> What holds people is the programme. A 2025 study monitored young adults’ brain activity and stress. It found that third places, the cafés and gathering spaces between home and work, had restorative effects comparable to green space, working mainly through social contact.<sup>23</sup>

That is why the Powerhouse has no fixed brief. Each one is entirely site-specific: placed where electric vehicle adoption is rising, and shaped by what that area lacks. Its programme might be a gym, a clinic, a drivers’ hostel or a market. Whatever it is, it is chosen for the people who live, work and travel nearby, and part of every site stays open to anyone.

For the same reason, the Powerhouse is not only for people who charge. The programme the community needs is the hook: it is what brings people to the site, on foot or by car. Charging is the outcome. It anchors the site, but it is not why people come. Seen this way, the Powerhouse is a first step towards a wider claim: that any parking lot or piece of dead space could be turned towards a programme that serves its area.
notes: Donald Shoup, The High Cost of Free Parking (Chicago: Planners Press, 2005).

Jerold S. Kayden, the New York City Department of City Planning and the Municipal Art Society of New York, Privately Owned Public Space: The New York City Experience (New York: John Wiley and Sons, 2000).
William H. Whyte, The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces (Washington, DC: Conservation Foundation, 1980).
Leiqing Xu et al., “Neurological Benefits of Third Places for Young Adults in Healthy Urban Environments,” Frontiers of Architectural Research 14 (2025): 1350–1363.

body: An anchor gives a place its reason to exist. The shopping mall made the idea explicit. When Victor Gruen designed Southdale outside Minneapolis in 1956, he hoped to give a new suburb the centre it lacked.<sup>24</sup> Two department stores at either end pulled shoppers through, and the rent from the smaller shops between them paid for the covered court where people met.<sup>25</sup> The anchor created the opportunity, and everything else grew around it.

At the Powerhouse the charger plays that part, though not by drawing the crowd. Charging needs a fixed stretch of time and a steady supply of energy, and it brings vehicles to the same place every day; that is what makes the site possible. The programme does the drawing. Paid programmes live off the people the site brings together, and their rent pays for energy generated on site, keeps charging and the free programmes free, and looks after the open ground. The mall’s anchor was a department store and its public space was private property. The Powerhouse is anchored by a piece of public infrastructure, and the place it supports is built for the community.
notes: M. Jeffrey Hardwick, Mall Maker: Victor Gruen, Architect of an American Dream (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2004).
Victor Gruen and Larry Smith, Shopping Towns USA: The Planning of Shopping Centers (New York: Reinhold, 1960).

body: This thesis argues that an Electric Vehicle Powerhouse complex will turn charging activities into an opportunity for enhanced civic / community engagements. Placed where electric vehicle adoption is rising, each Powerhouse turns idle parking into a civic amenity with a programme the area lacks: the programme is the hook, and charging is the outcome. If the extra time leads only to more retail, the hypothesis fails.

Three questions test the argument, and each becomes a chapter. The first is about the stay: how long each kind of vehicle stops, from a quick charge to an overnight rest, and what that time allows. The second is about public space: how much of a roadside site is given to community use, measured as a share of site area and leaving out parking and charging bays. The third is about the programme: what each neighbourhood lacks, which programmes are free and which are paid, and whether together they give people a reason to stay.

The research starts in New York, where electric vehicle adoption is rising. It then widens to the rest of the United States, with precedents from the United Kingdom, Europe and Japan. Its ground is the parking lot and other dead space. It covers every road vehicle, and the people nearby who do not charge at all. The stay it plans for runs from a twenty-minute charge to a driver’s overnight rest, by cable or wireless pad. Chargers at existing malls and supermarkets are set aside, because there shopping draws the charger rather than the other way round. Faster charging does not undo the argument. BYD’s megawatt chargers promise hundreds of kilometres of range in five minutes,<sup>26</sup> but at the Powerhouse it is the programme, not the charge, that holds people. Few site plans are public and operators guard their finances, so the funding model is argued from municipal and community-energy precedents: the rent of paid programmes keeps charging and the free programmes free.
notes: L. Zhang, K. Sun, and M. Nehrir, “Megawatt-Scale Charging Stations for Commercial Fleets: Grid Impacts and Ultra-Fast Energy Storage Interfacing,” IEEE Transactions on Power Systems 39, no. 3 (2024): 4120–4132.

body: The thesis reads the Powerhouse through three lenses, each concerned with one part of its argument: sustainability with the Powerhouse and its charging, phenomenology with the stop, and social theory with the community and its public space.

The first lens is sustainability. Sustainable development is usually defined as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own.<sup>27</sup> Here it has three parts. Environmentally, the Powerhouse builds on ground that parking already covers and makes and stores its own energy. Socially, it serves people who cannot charge at home and stays open to those who do not charge at all. Economically, its programme keeps the place running. Ian McHarg’s practice of reading a site in layers, and Sim Van der Ryn and Stuart Cowan’s principle that design should grow from its place and make natural systems visible, guide where a Powerhouse goes and how its energy is shown.<sup>28</sup>

The second lens is phenomenology: what it is like to spend the stop on site. Martin Heidegger argued that to build is to make dwelling possible, and that a built thing, like a bridge, gathers a place around it.<sup>29</sup> The charger can do the same. Christian Norberg-Schulz added that people need to know where they are and to feel that they belong,<sup>30</sup> which today’s identical charging stops rarely allow. In these terms, the Powerhouse turns a pause in a journey into a place.

The third lens is social theory. Henri Lefebvre showed that space is produced: planned by those who design it and lived by those who use it.<sup>31</sup> Charging sites today are almost entirely planned, by standards and operators, for the vehicle. Lefebvre’s right to the city, the claim that everyone may use and shape urban space,<sup>32</sup> underlies the Powerhouse’s promise of public space open to all. Michel Foucault’s account of surveillance raises the opposite risk, that such places watch and move on the people who linger.<sup>33</sup> The Powerhouse answers with Jane Jacobs’s alternative: safety that comes from people being present, not from being watched.<sup>34</sup>
notes: World Commission on Environment and Development, Our Common Future (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1987), 43.
Ian L. McHarg, Design with Nature (Garden City, NY: Natural History Press, 1969); Sim Van der Ryn and Stuart Cowan, Ecological Design (Washington, DC: Island Press, 1996).
Martin Heidegger, “Building Dwelling Thinking,” in Poetry, Language, Thought, trans. Albert Hofstadter (New York: Harper & Row, 1971).
Christian Norberg-Schulz, Genius Loci: Towards a Phenomenology of Architecture (New York: Rizzoli, 1980).
Henri Lefebvre, The Production of Space, trans. Donald Nicholson-Smith (Oxford: Blackwell, 1991).
Henri Lefebvre, “The Right to the City,” in Writings on Cities, ed. and trans. Eleonore Kofman and Elizabeth Lebas (Oxford: Blackwell, 1996).
Michel Foucault, Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison, trans. Alan Sheridan (New York: Pantheon, 1977).
Jane Jacobs, The Death and Life of Great American Cities (New York: Random House, 1961).

body: The thesis is built in four layers: a question, a hypothesis, three lenses, and a sequence of chapters that tests the hypothesis and leads to a design.

The question is what a charging site could become if it were designed for the people who stop there rather than only for their vehicles. The hypothesis answers it: an Electric Vehicle Powerhouse complex will turn charging activities into an opportunity for enhanced civic / community engagements. It has three parts, and each becomes a chapter. The community stop is the time people spend on site, set by the vehicle, the charger and the law. The public space is the share of the site anyone can use without buying anything. The programme is what the neighbourhood lacks, built around the charge.
The three lenses set out in section VII run through every part: sustainability for the ground and the energy, phenomenology for the experience of the stop, and social theory for who the space is for.

The method is comparative. Rather than build a site and wait to see what happens, the thesis studies existing ones: gas stations, highway service areas, truck stops and charging hubs, in corridor, city and town settings. At each it records three things: how long people stay, how much of the site is open to them, and whether a programme serves them while they wait. The evidence comes from published specifications, site plans and aerial photographs, timed observation on site, short conversations with the people there, and first-person notes on what the stop is like.

The chapters follow this structure. Chapter 2, The Stop, defines and measures the time on site, through sustainability and phenomenology. Chapter 3, The Public Space, asks what makes people stay and what each neighbourhood needs, through phenomenology and social theory. Chapter 4, The Programme, asks how a programme can serve people and keep a place running without taking it over, through social theory and sustainability. Together they test the hypothesis.

What the chapters find becomes a set of design criteria. In Graduate Thesis 01 and 02 these are applied to a chosen site, where the Powerhouse is designed as a working building: chargers, energy, programme and public space arranged for one neighbourhood. The written thesis makes the case; the design shows what it looks like.

Every way of travelling makes people wait, and every kind of wait has produced its own place. A rider who walks up to a bus stop waits about eight and a half minutes on average.<sup>1</sup> A driver at a gas station stays about five. A passenger at a large American airport spends a median of around eighty minutes in the terminal.<sup>2</sup> Each wait is sized to what the journey asks of it, and the building around it follows.

The private car is different. It is not waiting for its passengers; they are waiting to use it. In 2022 a typical American household vehicle stood parked for 95 per cent of the day and was driven for about sixty-five minutes.<sup>3</sup> That idle time is what makes the private electric car easy to charge. Most owners plug in at home and charge overnight while they sleep, and about four of every five charges happen this way.<sup>4</sup> For a driver with a driveway, the stop barely exists.

Not every vehicle can wait for night. Buses, taxis, ride-hail cars, delivery vans and trucks work all day. A full-time ride-hail car covers 180 to 190 miles a day,<sup>5</sup> against about fifty for a car in a one-car household,<sup>6</sup> and many ride-hail drivers live in apartments with no off-street parking. New York is electrifying exactly these fleets. The city’s Taxi and Limousine Commission aims to make the vast majority of its licensed vehicles electric by 2030.<sup>7</sup> The MTA is committed to a zero-emission bus fleet by 2040, though its first electric buses could not get through a full day of service.<sup>8</sup> Trucks, as Chapter 1 showed, stop by law. These vehicles have to charge during the working day, away from home, and that is where the stop is made.

New York makes this case more sharply than anywhere else in the country. Across the United States, 69 per cent of workers drive to work alone; in New York State the figure is 49 per cent, the lowest of any state.<sup>9</sup> The rest ride buses, trains, taxis and ride-hail cars, or walk and cycle, and more of their journeys are made in vehicles that someone else owns and that never sleep in a driveway.

The public charging stop is therefore for four groups of people. The first is fleets charging mid-shift. The second is drivers without a driveway: half of New York City’s car owners park on the street.<sup>10</sup> The third is travellers far from home. The fourth is the people nearby who come for the programme rather than the charge. This chapter is about the stop they share: what it is, how long it lasts, and what sets its length. It moves from the ground the stop occupies, to the network it belongs to, to the history of stops that became places, and then to the three things that set a stop’s length today: the vehicle, the law and the speed of the charger. Of the three lenses set out in Chapter 1, it works mainly through two. Sustainability looks at the ground charging occupies and the energy it needs. Phenomenology looks at the stop as time that is lived, not just measured.<sup>11</sup>
notes: Wei Fan and Zhi-Chao Liu, “Passenger Waiting Time and Perceived Transit Service Quality: Quantitative Evaluation of Real-Time Information,” Transportation Research Record: Journal of the Transportation Research Board 2674, no. 9 (2020): 112–124.

body: American cities have covered a large share of their land in concrete, and most of it is for parking. Donald Shoup showed that free parking is paid for by everyone, in higher rents, higher prices and land that could have been used for something else.<sup>12</sup> The curb, the private lot, the gas station forecourt, the supermarket car park and the highway rest area are all versions of the same ground: paved space sized to the vehicle, not to the person in it.

New York shows what that ground does over a day. About 1.6 million people sleep in Manhattan; on a weekday about 3.1 million are there.<sup>13</sup> They come in by train and bus, and by road. Around 490,000 vehicles enter Manhattan below 60th Street each day,<sup>14</sup> carrying about 785,000 people in private cars,<sup>15</sup> while taxis and ride-hail cars make close to a million trips a day across the city.<sup>16</sup> The core’s roughly 103,000 off-street parking spaces fill as they arrive.<sup>17</sup>

Each of those vehicles already stops. A commuter’s car sits in a garage for eight or ten hours, long enough for a slow charge to fill it. A taxi or ride-hail car pauses between trips, long enough for a fast one. A bus waits at its layover, and a delivery van waits while it loads. As these vehicles go electric, the question is not where to build new stops but how to charge during the ones they already make, in the city, where they are. The Powerhouse does not replace the concrete. It is a layer added to it: paved ground that already exists, given a programme the area lacks, with charging as the outcome.

What matters, then, is the length of the stop. In this thesis it is defined as the time in minutes between a person arriving at a site and leaving it, on a visit whose main purpose is to charge a vehicle or to take a required rest. I call this the stop. Parking is the starting condition: the ground the stop already sits on, and the ground the Powerhouse proposes to give back. Reusing it, rather than paving new land, is the first sense in which the Powerhouse is sustainable: a solution that grows from the place it is in.<sup>18</sup>
notes: Donald Shoup, The High Cost of Free Parking (Chicago: Planners Press, 2005).
NYU Rudin Center for Transportation, The Dynamic Population of Manhattan (New York: NYU Wagner, 2012).
New York Metropolitan Transportation Council (NYMTC), Hub-Bound Travel Data: Vehicles Entering Manhattan Central Business District South of 60th Street (New York: NYMTC, 2024).
New York Metropolitan Transportation Council, Hub Bound Travel Data 2024.
New York City Taxi and Limousine Commission, 2025 trip totals, testimony on the preliminary budget, March 2026.
New York City Department of City Planning, Manhattan Core Public Parking Study (2011).
Sim Van der Ryn and Stuart Cowan, Ecological Design (Washington, DC: Island Press, 1996).

body: Charging is not one place but a network, and each part of it produces a different kind of stop. It helps to read it as an anatomy, from the slowest charger to the fastest.

Home and workplace. Most charging happens where the vehicle is already parked for hours. A car plugged into a wall socket or a home charger fills slowly overnight, and an office car park does the same during the working day. By the Department of Energy’s estimate, about four in five charges happen at home.19 These charges create no stop at all, because the vehicle was going to be standing there anyway.
Destination charging. Slower public chargers at supermarkets, hotels, car parks and on the street let people top up while they do something else. The stop is set by the errand, not by the charge.

Fast charging. Along highways and in city hubs, fast chargers fill a car in well under an hour. This is where the stop is created by the charge itself. The driver is there because the car needs energy, and has to wait for it. It is the closest thing to the gas station, and the clearest case for the Powerhouse.

Freight and fleet charging. Trucks, buses and delivery vans charge at depots overnight or at high-power chargers along freight routes. Freight already has a stop it cannot avoid: drivers are required by law to rest, and the places to do so are short. The lack of truck parking is one of the most pressing problems in American trucking, and drivers near the end of their legal hours keep driving to look for a space.20

Battery swapping. For scooters, and for some cars and trucks, the empty battery can be taken out and replaced with a full one. The vehicle stops for minutes, but the battery it leaves behind still has to be charged somewhere.

This anatomy creates the first problem for measuring the stop. Because most charging happens at home, the people at public chargers are a particular group: travellers on long trips, people who live in apartments or park on the street, ride-hail drivers and fleets. They are not a cross-section of all drivers, and a study of them alone could give a false picture. This is a problem of selection bias. The study responds by choosing sites that serve different users, such as a highway site used by travellers and trucks, a city hub used by residents and ride-hail drivers, and a small-town site used by local people, and by asking each visitor why they are there. It also counts people who arrive without a vehicle, since the Powerhouse is meant to be open to everyone.
notes: US Department of Energy, “National EV Charging Network,” https://www.energy.gov/topics/national-ev-charging-network.

Nana Duah, Steven Jiang, Om Prakash Yadav, Hieu Trung Nguyen, and Nastasha Earle-Young, “Navigating the Truck Parking Challenge: A Comprehensive Review of Strategies, Emerging Technologies, and Future Directions,” Transportation Research Interdisciplinary Perspectives 34 (2025): 101740, 2.

body: The link between the stop and the making of a place is old, and Chapter 1 traced it from Charles Horton Cooley’s observation of 1894 that “population and wealth tend to collect wherever there is a break in transportation.”<sup>21</sup> What matters here is how differently each type treated the person. The railway station and the airport were built around the wait, filling it with halls, shops and restaurants.<sup>22</sup> The gas station went the other way, and it barely changed for a century.<sup>23</sup> It was built for the vehicle, and the person was expected to leave as soon as possible.

The Powerhouse proposes a new type in this line: a station for electric road transport. Like the railway station, it is organised around a break in the journey. Unlike the gas station, it is designed for the person as well as the vehicle. It also has a second purpose. By making charging somewhere people want to be, it makes the switch to electric vehicles easier to choose. In phenomenological terms, it turns a pause in a journey into a place: somewhere to dwell for the length of the stop, rather than a queue to get through.<sup>24</sup>

This history suggests the method. The study does not control the length of the stop; nobody can make a car charge more slowly to see what happens. It is comparative instead. It selects existing sites where the stop is short, medium, long and overnight, and compares how much of each site is given to people. This follows the building-type studies of Pevsner and Geist introduced in Chapter 1: follow one type through many examples and look for what changes with the conditions.<sup>25</sup> The stop is therefore measured rather than manipulated, and the sites are chosen to cover its full range.

The history also warns of the most serious problem. The hypothesis says a longer stop leads to more public space, but the reverse can also be true. People stay longer at stations and service areas that give them somewhere to sit and something to eat, and truck drivers choose rest areas with better amenities and safety features.<sup>26</sup> If the study only observed that sites with more public space have longer stops, it could not tell which caused which. This is a threat to internal validity. The response is to take the length of the stop from the charger, the vehicle and the law, which are fixed before anyone decides what to build around them, and to use the time people actually stay as a check.
notes: Charles Horton Cooley, “The Theory of Transportation,” Publications of the American Economic Association 9, no. 3 (1894): 91.
Carroll L. V. Meeks, The Railroad Station: An Architectural History (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1956).
John A. Jakle and Keith A. Sculle, The Gas Station in America (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1994).

Martin Heidegger, “Building Dwelling Thinking,” in Poetry, Language, Thought, trans. Albert Hofstadter (New York: Harper & Row, 1971); Yi-Fu Tuan, Space and Place: The Perspective of Experience (Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press, 1977), 6.
Nikolaus Pevsner, A History of Building Types (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1976); Johann Friedrich Geist, Arcades: The History of a Building Type (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1983).
Duah et al., “Navigating the Truck Parking Challenge,” 9.

body: The length of the stop depends first on what arrives. Charging time is set by two numbers: how much energy the battery holds, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh), and how fast the charger can deliver it, measured in kilowatts (kW). Dividing the first by the second gives a rough time. A 75 kWh car battery charged from 10 to 80 percent needs about 52 kWh. At 100 kW that takes about half an hour; at 50 kW, about an hour; on a 7 kW home charger, most of a working day.<sup>27</sup> Small vehicles need little energy and can charge from a wall socket. Trucks sit at the far end. Anderson and Kish note that charging an electric truck can take up to eight hours, while refuelling a diesel truck takes “a mere five to ten minutes.”<sup>28</sup> Table 2.1 sets out the range.

The table groups the stop into four lengths. A short stop is under fifteen minutes. A medium stop is fifteen minutes to an hour, which is a car at a fast charger. A long stop is one to three hours, typical of buses, large vehicles and trucks at fast chargers. An overnight stop is eight hours or more. These lengths match the lengths of stay used in Chapter 4 to choose a programme for the site.

Charge time, however, is not the same as waiting time. A car may need forty minutes of charge, but the driver may leave after twenty because they have enough to get home, or stay long after it finishes because they are eating. Some drivers never leave the car and spend the stop on their phones. If the study measured only the charge, it would describe the machine, not the person. This is a problem of construct validity.

The response is simple. The study records both: the time the vehicle needs to charge, worked out from Table 2.1, and the time people actually stay, observed on site using the timed counts developed by William Whyte and by Jan Gehl and Birgitte Svarre.<sup>29</sup> The difference between the two is the point. A charging site that only holds people for as long as the charge takes is still a forecourt. The Powerhouse aims for people to stay longer than they have to, because the place is worth staying in. Observation is kept consistent by visiting each site at the same times of day, over several days, and nobody is identified.
notes: Author’s calculation: 70 percent of a 75 kWh battery is 52.5 kWh; 52.5 kWh at 100 kW is about 32 minutes, at 50 kW about 63 minutes, and at 7 kW about 7.5 hours.
Anne-Marie Anderson and Richard J. Kish, “The Costs and Benefits of Electric Trucks: A Synopsis of the U.S. Trucking Market,” Sustainability 17, no. 5 (2025): 2097, 5.
William H. Whyte, The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces (Washington, DC: Conservation Foundation, 1980); Jan Gehl and Birgitte Svarre, How to Study Public Life (Washington, DC: Island Press, 2013).

body: For professional drivers, the length of the stop is set partly by law rather than technology. In the United States a truck driver may drive no more than eleven hours after ten consecutive hours off duty, and must take a thirty-minute break after eight hours of driving.<sup>30</sup> In the European Union a driver of a truck or coach must take a break of at least forty-five minutes after four and a half hours at the wheel, and a daily rest of at least eleven hours, which may be shortened to nine.<sup>31</sup> Table 2.2 places these rules in the same four lengths as the vehicles.

These rules apply however fast the truck charges. A required rest that coincides with a required charge is a long stop that is very likely to happen, which makes freight the most stable case for this study and the first one it tests.

Charger standards set the stop for cars. The federal National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure standards require funded highway stations to offer at least four fast-charging ports, each able to deliver 150 kilowatts at the same time.<sup>32</sup> That figure is a practical baseline for highway stops over the next decade, because it is what public money is building, and it is the figure used to calculate the charge time at highway sites.

Zoning decides what may be built around the charger. Local codes were largely written for gas stations and parking lots, and they shape whether a charging site can include food, seating, workspace or rooms to stay. The Powerhouse does not fit those categories. It is not a plaza added to a car park; it works like a third place with charging at its centre, which is a different way of using the ground altogether. Its programme comes from the needs of the area around it. On a highway or freight corridor it might be somewhere to stay, with rooms and showers for drivers on their required rest. In a city it might be a gym or a place to work. In a town without one, it might be a medical centre.

This affects how much of the site is given to people more than the length of the stop itself, and it is taken up in Chapters 3 and 4. For this chapter, zoning matters because two sites with the same stop may give very different amounts of ground to people simply because one is allowed to and the other is not. The study records the zoning of each site so that its effect is not mistaken for the effect of the stop.
notes: Maximum Driving Time for Property-Carrying Vehicles, 49 C.F.R. § 395.3.

Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the harmonisation of certain social legislation relating to road transport, Official Journal of the European Union L 102 (2006), arts. 7–8.
Federal Highway Administration, “National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Standards and Requirements,” 23 C.F.R. pt. 680 (2023).

body: The stop is a moving target. Charging is getting faster. In 2025 BYD announced a one-megawatt “flash charging” system that it claims adds around 400 kilometres of range in five minutes.<sup>33</sup> Battery swapping points the same way, replacing a whole battery in minutes. If these spread, the car stop could fall back towards the length of a fuel stop within the life of the buildings this thesis proposes. Cooley saw something similar with the railways: as transfers improved, small breaks disappeared. In his words, “the number of breaks represents the expense of transportation.”<sup>34</sup>

That does not undo the thesis. A faster stop for the driver does not mean less charging overall. The energy still has to come from somewhere, and a battery swapped out of a vehicle in five minutes still needs hours to recharge. Flash charging at a megawatt draws on the grid far harder than a slow charger, and needs storage and supply close by. The Powerhouse can be that place: the swap centre where batteries are held and recharged, and the local source of power, generating and storing its own electricity for the vehicles around it. It is meant to be a powerhouse in the literal sense, solving transport’s need for electricity as well as the person’s need for somewhere to be. This is the sustainability lens at its most literal: the site produces energy as well as using it.<sup>35</sup>

Stan Allen’s account of “infrastructural urbanism” and the lineage of heroic transport monuments—from McKim, Mead & White’s Pennsylvania Station to Santiago Calatrava’s grand railway cathedrals (Lisbon’s Gare do Oriente, Liège-Guillemins, and the World Trade Center Oculus)—show that the greatest infrastructural hubs are never mere storage or utilitarian service sheds. They are architectural marvels: soaring civic stations that celebrate human transit, dramatize engineering, and dignify the public domain.36 Rather than looking at adaptive reuse or retrofitting an existing multi-storey garage, the Powerhouse establishes a new civic station typology: a purpose-designed monumental nexus engineered for the electric age. Its muscular structural ribs, expressive vaults, and daylight-flooded concourses turn the mechanical pause of charging into an inspiring civic threshold for New York, integrating multi-megawatt battery reserves, rapid fleet turnaround, and vibrant neighborhood life under a singular monumental shell (Table 2.3).

This also changes what the stop depends on. If the charge no longer forces people to stay, they will stay only where the site gives them a reason, which is the role of the programme, and why the hypothesis does not rest on charging time alone. The study allows for this in three ways. It puts most weight on the stops that technology does not control, such as the required rest for drivers, which will still apply when a truck can charge in minutes. It uses the four lengths of stop rather than exact minutes, so a site only has to stay within the same range. And it asks which parts of the programme would still work if the stop were halved. Because the Powerhouse is a charging hub, energy store and third place at once, it can adapt as vehicles and charging change, rather than becoming obsolete with them.
Summary

The stop is where this thesis begins: the time a person spends at a site whose main purpose is to charge a vehicle or take a required rest. It sits on ground that parking already occupies, within a network where most charging happens at home, and it continues a long history in which the break in a journey became a place. Its length is set by the vehicle, the law and the speed of the charger, and it ranges from a few minutes to most of a day. The study compares existing sites across four lengths of stop, recording both the time the charge needs and the time people actually stay.

The main challenges are that public-charger users are not typical drivers, that a good site can lengthen the stop as well as respond to it, that charge time is not the same as time on site, that zoning can shape a site as much as the stop does, and that faster charging may shorten the stop. The responses are to study different kinds of sites and users, to take the stop from the charger, vehicle and law and use observation as a check, to record the person as well as the plug, to note each site’s zoning, and to rest the argument on required breaks and ranges of stop rather than on charger speed. Even as charging gets faster, the Powerhouse remains a source of power for transport and a place worth stopping in. Read through sustainability, the stop sits on reused ground and draws on energy made on site; read through phenomenology, it is time that can be lived rather than waited out. Chapter 3 turns to that place, through phenomenology and social theory.
notes: L. Zhang, K. Sun, and M. Nehrir, “Megawatt-Scale Charging Stations for Commercial Fleets: Grid Impacts and Ultra-Fast Energy Storage Interfacing,” IEEE Transactions on Power Systems 39, no. 3 (2024): 4120–4132.
Cooley, “The Theory of Transportation,” 99.
John Tillman Lyle, Regenerative Design for Sustainable Development (New York: John Wiley & Sons, 1994).
Stan Allen, “Infrastructural Urbanism,” in Points + Lines: Diagrams and Projects for the City (New York: Princeton Architectural Press, 1999), 46–57.

body: Chapter 2 established that electric road transport brings back a substantial daily pause, and that this pause sits on paved ground cities have already given to parking. Time on site, however, is only an opportunity. Whether a charging stop becomes a civic place depends on how that ground is held, who is allowed to use it, and what kind of life it supports. This chapter examines the public space of the Powerhouse through phenomenology and social theory: how hard utility infrastructure can fuse with social infrastructure, how monumental civic terminals can belong to their towns and neighbourhoods, and how transport infrastructure can return land to the city rather than dividing it.

Infrastructure is not only pipes, cables and roads; it is also the physical places where people meet. Sociologist Eric Klinenberg calls these places—libraries, parks, playgrounds, community rooms and even neighbourhood barbershops—social infrastructure: the material settings that shape whether strangers cross paths, build trust and help one another.1 In his study of the 1995 Chicago heat wave, neighbourhoods with the same demographics and temperatures suffered vastly different death tolls; the neighbourhoods with active libraries, commercial streets, community organisations and public gathering places lost far fewer residents because neighbours knew and checked on one another.2

Hard infrastructure moves energy, water and vehicles. Social infrastructure holds a community together. Modern cities almost always build and fund the two apart: utility authorities and charging networks build closed technical compounds, while civic departments struggle to fund and maintain public rooms. The Powerhouse fuses the two in one building: charging, transit and local energy generation on one side, and a neighbourhood room, civic programme and open public ground on the other.
notes: Eric Klinenberg, Palaces for the People: How Social Infrastructure Can Help Fight Inequality, Polarization, and the Decline of Civic Life (New York: Crown, 2018).
Eric Klinenberg, Heat Wave: A Social Autopsy of Disaster in Chicago (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 2002); Klinenberg, Palaces for the People, 1–24.

body: The clearest working precedent for a roadside stop that belongs to its town is Japan’s network of Michi-no-eki (“road stations”). Since 1993 Japan’s Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism has designated more than 1,200 public roadside stations across the country.3 Every station is required to provide three functions at once: 24-hour free parking, toilets and rest for travellers; road, emergency and local tourist information; and regional promotion facilities—farmers’ markets for local produce, restaurants, craft workshops, community halls and event plazas—planned and operated jointly by the road authority and the host municipality.

Because each Michi-no-eki is co-owned with its municipality, no two are identical, and residents use them as everyday third places even when they are not travelling. Many are also equipped with backup power, water storage and open staging ground so that they double as neighbourhood disaster-relief bases after earthquakes or typhoons. Where commercial electric forecourts treat the driver as a customer waiting for a battery to fill, the Michi-no-eki treats the stop as a civic threshold between the road network and the community.
notes: Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT), Japan, “Michi-no-Eki (Roadside Stations),” launched 1993.

body: Standardised charging canopies dropped onto asphalt lots erase local character, treating the city as an afterthought. Creating an architectural marvel does the opposite: it elevates the energy transition into a monumental civic station that gathers a world around it, achieving what Christian Norberg-Schulz called genius loci—a distinct architectural character rooted in civic permanence—and what Martin Heidegger described as the capacity of a monumental built work to gather a world around it.4 Just as the grand railway terminals of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries (such as McKim, Mead & White’s Pennsylvania Station) and Santiago Calatrava’s kinetic rail monuments (such as Gare do Oriente in Lisbon, Liège-Guillemins, and Zurich Stadelhofen) turned infrastructural necessity into civic pride, the Powerhouse invents a new station typology. It replaces the utilitarian asphalt lot with a breathtaking structural nexus of daylight, expressive ribbed vaults, and generous civic halls. Rather than hiding behind functionalism or settling for adaptive compromises, the Powerhouse asserts that New York’s charging infrastructure must become an inspiring public room for all citizens.

The history of transport architecture reveals that great infrastructural hubs have always been defined by monumental civic ambition rather than utilitarian expediency. Santiago Calatrava’s grand railway cathedrals—such as the Gare do Oriente in Lisbon (1998), the Liège-Guillemins railway station in Belgium (2009), Zurich Stadelhofen, and the World Trade Center Oculus in New York—demonstrate how expressive skeletal arches, kinetic skylights, and expansive column-free concourses elevate the act of waiting into an awe-inspiring civic ritual.<sup>5</sup> Similarly, McKim, Mead & White’s Pennsylvania Station (1910) and Grand Central Terminal proved that arrival in a metropolis should occur through an inspiring civic gateway.<sup>6</sup> The Powerhouse adopts this heroic lineage: it is not a compromised garage retrofit or an asphalt charging lot, but a purpose-designed monumental civic station for the 21st-century electric transition.
notes: Martin Heidegger, “Building Dwelling Thinking,” in Poetry, Language, Thought, trans. Albert Hofstadter (New York: Harper & Row, 1971); Christian Norberg-Schulz, Genius Loci: Towards a Phenomenology of Architecture (New York: Rizzoli, 1980).
Santiago Calatrava, Gare do Oriente (Lisbon, 1998) and Liège-Guillemins Station (Belgium, 2009); Philip Jodidio, Santiago Calatrava: Complete Works 1979–Present (Cologne: Taschen, 2022).
Carroll L. V. Meeks, The Railroad Station: An Architectural History (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1956); Carl W. Condit, The Port of New York (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1980).

body: Energy infrastructure has traditionally been hidden behind perimeter fences, warning signs and blank facades. When an energy facility must sit inside a city, however, its mass and roof can give space back to the public. Bjarke Ingels Group’s CopenHill (Amager Bakke, Copenhagen, 2019)—a 41,000-square-metre waste-to-energy power plant built for Amager Ressourcecenter, a company owned by five surrounding municipalities—arranged its internal machinery in height order from tallest to shortest so that the roof could form a continuous 85-metre slope.<sup>7</sup>

That roof is now a public mountain in a flat city: 500 metres of artificial ski runs, a landscaped hiking and running trail, the world’s tallest artificial climbing wall on the facade, a rooftop café and a viewing platform. A glazed elevator shaft rising alongside the stack lets visitors look directly into the plant’s operating halls on their way to the roof. People come to ski, climb or walk and leave knowing how their city’s energy is made. The Powerhouse applies the same principle—what BIG calls hedonistic sustainability—to the electric transition: if a neighbourhood needs high-capacity charging, battery storage and solar generation, the roof and ground of that plant should be a public park and gathering place.
notes: Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG), CopenHill / Amager Bakke Waste-to-Energy Plant, Copenhagen (completed 2019).

body: Whether a space is truly public is decided not only by its walls, but by its rules. In Extrastatecraft (2014), architectural theorist Keller Easterling argues that infrastructure is the hidden operating system of the modern city: technical standards, spatial layouts, payment gates and software protocols quietly determine who may enter and what they may do long before any formal law is invoked.8

A charging station that can only be entered in a private car, unlocked through a smartphone app, paid for with a credit card, and occupied while a vehicle is plugged in has already written its social rules: anyone without a car, a bank account or a transaction to make is a trespasser. Even well-designed urban spaces fail when their rules exclude the surrounding public. The Powerhouse makes its operating rules visible and civic: its plazas, toilets, seating, shade and community halls are open to everyone, with no purchase required and no vehicle needed.
notes: Keller Easterling, Extrastatecraft: The Power of Infrastructure Space (London: Verso, 2014).

body: Transport corridors—rail cuts, elevated viaducts, arterial highways and garage rows—often act as scars that sever one neighbourhood from another. Across the past two decades, a series of urban projects has shown how reclaiming transport land can turn that scar into a civic seam. In New York, the High Line (2009) transformed a disused elevated freight railway into a linear public park; in Madrid, Madrid Río (2011) buried the M-30 ring motorway beneath ten kilometres of riverside parkland and footbridges; and in Torrelavega, Spain, Manuel Villalaín González and Manuel Mateu Sanchís’s Europan 17 winning project “Cicatrice” (2023) reclaims roughly 50,000 square metres freed by placing the railway underground to stitch the divided city back together around a new civic centre.<sup>9</sup>

The Powerhouse works at the same threshold. By placing public entrances, vertical circulation and shared plazas across the grade changes and edges of road and rail corridors, it turns the back door of transport infrastructure into a neighbourhood front door.
notes: James Corner Field Operations and Diller Scofidio + Renfro, The High Line, New York (opened 2009); Burgos & Garrido, Porras La Casta, Rubio & Álvarez-Sala, and West 8, Madrid Río (completed 2011); Manuel Villalaín González and Manuel Mateu Sanchís, “Cicatrice,” Torrelavega, Europan 17 (2023).

body: Public space stays alive when people have a recurring reason to use it. Chapter 3 showed that a charging stop can become social infrastructure if it is open without purchase and stitched into the fabric of its neighbourhood. Chapter 4 asks how the building is programmed, how it is paid for, and how it works across the twenty-four hours of the day. Working through social theory and sustainability, it brings together four ideas: the multimodal mobility hub with a civic room at its heart, the right of non-drivers and residents to shape the programme, the energy commons that lets local power and charging revenue sustain community uses, and the temporal rhythm that keeps the building active across every shift.

When a charging site is planned for cars alone, it isolates drivers from every other way people move. Planned instead as a neighbourhood mobility hub, it brings train, bus, bicycle, micromobility, walking, ride-hail and EV charging together around a shared civic room. In London, Foster + Partners’ Crossrail Place at Canary Wharf (2015) topped a new Elizabeth line railway station with four storeys of community rooms, shops and a public roof garden under a 310-metre timber lattice, uniting station, park and public hall in one section.1 Across Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium, municipal networks such as Bremen’s mobil.punkt hubs place car-sharing, cargo bikes, cycle parking, transit stops and neighbourhood services at a single street corner, while Carlos Moreno’s model of the “15-minute city” argues that daily essentials—work, food, healthcare, learning and leisure—should sit within a short walk or bike ride of every home.2
notes: Foster + Partners, Crossrail Place, Canary Wharf, London (completed 2015).

City of Bremen, mobil.punkt neighbourhood mobility hubs (2003–present); Carlos Moreno, Zaheer Allam, Didier Chabaud, Catherine Gall, and Florent Pratlong, “Introducing the ‘15-Minute City’: Sustainability, Resilience and Place Identity in Future Post-Pandemic Cities,” Smart Cities 4, no. 1 (2021): 93–111.

body: Henri Lefebvre’s “right to the city” is not merely the right to visit existing urban spaces, but the right of inhabitants to appropriate and shape the places of daily life outside the logic of commodity exchange.<sup>3</sup> Applied to transport infrastructure, it means a neighbourhood charging hub cannot be programmed solely around what extracts the highest spend per minute from a captive driver.

Instead, the programme is chosen by auditing what the surrounding radius lacks. Where a neighbourhood is underserved by healthcare, fresh food, study space or youth facilities, the Powerhouse allocates floor area to a community clinic, a fresh-produce market, a library reading room or after-school studios alongside commercial anchor tenants.
notes: Henri Lefebvre, “The Right to the City,” in Writings on Cities, ed. and trans. Eleonore Kofman and Elizabeth Lebas (Oxford: Blackwell, 1996), 147–159.

body: Because different vehicles and errands bring different people, the Powerhouse serves overlapping publics that rarely share a building today: morning rail and bus commuters, long-haul and local delivery drivers taking mandated rest breaks, ride-hail and taxi drivers between shifts, apartment residents charging a car or e-bike, schoolchildren in the afternoon, and older residents visiting a clinic or park.

Designing for all of them in one section turns Jane Jacobs’s principle of “eyes on the street” into an interior and rooftop condition: a charging deck or rest stop that would feel isolated and unsafe at night becomes active and self-policing when it shares its hall with a 24-hour community and mobility hub.<sup>4</sup>
notes: Jane Jacobs, The Death and Life of Great American Cities (New York: Random House, 1961), 35–54.

body: How does a charging hub fund public space and community rooms without turning into a shopping mall? The answer lies in treating local energy generation and charging as an energy commons: infrastructure owned in whole or in part by the public and the community it serves.

Three models show how this works in practice. First, municipal ownership: CopenHill in Copenhagen was built for an energy company owned by five local municipalities, allowing capital investment in clean energy to deliver a major public park on its roof.5 Second, community equity shares: in the South Bronx, the MN8 Gateway to Hunts Point freight-charging hub (scheduled for ~2029) pairs high-power commercial truck and car charging with a community solar array serving roughly 300 local households, structured so that 50 percent of the project is community-owned.6 Third, neighbourhood microgrids: projects such as the Brooklyn Microgrid allow rooftop solar producers and battery hosts to trade local electricity directly with neighbours and feed resilience power back into the local grid during peak demand.7 At the Powerhouse, rooftop solar, stationary battery storage and commercial fast-charging fees cross-subsidise free civic space and affordable community rooms.
notes: Amager Ressourcecenter (ARC), municipal waste-to-energy partnership of Dragør, Frederiksberg, Hvidovre, København and Tårnby, Copenhagen.
MN8 Energy, “MN8 Energy Announces Gateway to Hunts Point Clean Freight and Community Solar Hub,” press release, July 23, 2025.
LO3 Energy / Brooklyn Microgrid, peer-to-peer community energy network, Brooklyn, New York.

body: Cities run on rhythms: morning commutes, school bells, delivery shifts, evening gatherings and overnight rest. In What Time Is This Place? (1972), Kevin Lynch urged architects and planners to treat time as a design material as real as space, and in Rhythmanalysis (2004), Henri Lefebvre showed how urban life is produced by the intersection of cyclical daily rhythms and linear work schedules.8

Most monofunctional buildings sit empty for half the twenty-four-hour cycle: office car parks empty at 6 pm, residential garages empty at 9 am, and highway forecourts go quiet overnight. By matching its programme to the four lengths of stop established in Chapter 2 and the four six-hour windows of the urban day, the Powerhouse stays active around the clock (Table 4.2).
notes: Kevin Lynch, What Time Is This Place? (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1972); Henri Lefebvre, Rhythmanalysis: Space, Time and Everyday Life, trans. Stuart Elden and Gerald Moore (London: Continuum, 2004).

body: A building designed for a twenty-to-sixty-minute stop must also be ready for a future in which batteries charge in five minutes or autonomous vehicles drop passengers at the door and park themselves elsewhere. As Stan Allen argued in “Infrastructural Urbanism,” architecture endures when it provides a robust spatial field whose servicing and structural grid can host changing programmes without demolition.<sup>9</sup>

Because the Powerhouse is conceived as a monumental civic station with soaring structural spans, vaulted ceiling heights, and integrated utility spines, its civic armature endures across evolutionary cycles: spaces dedicated to rapid fleet charging today can seamlessly rebalance into expanded public atriums, community fabrication labs, or grid-scale battery chambers as autonomous operations and solid-state charging accelerate.
Summary

The Powerhouse elevates the technical necessity of electric vehicle fast charging into an inspiring architectural marvel and civic station for New York. Anchored by a multimodal transit cathedral, governed by open public rules, sustained by a community energy commons, and programmed across all twenty-four hours of the day, it transforms a technical pause in transport into lasting monumental infrastructure.
notes: Stan Allen, “Infrastructural Urbanism,” in Points + Lines: Diagrams and Projects for the City (New York: Princeton Architectural Press, 1999), 46–57.
